role: Main analysis script: builds the interval records, runs integrity checks, writes facts.json and FACTS.md.
purpose: This script reads the raw result files and builds one record with the rate in GB/s per timed interval: every interval of the rerun, and selected intervals of the earlier runs. It then runs 27 integrity checks, gets the statistics and the text from `facts_text.py`, and writes `S/facts.json` and `S/FACTS.md` when every check passes.

main_flow.step: The script imports `facts_data.py` under the name `fd` and takes the folder names `R` and `S` from it. It sets four constants: the paths of the two driver logs (`GO_LOG`, `GO2_LOG`), the filter `POS01` and the kernel list `READ3`.
When the file is run as a script, Python calls `main`. The script takes one optional argument, `--print`. This file reads no environment variable.

`main` calls `collect` (line 1035). `collect` first reads the machine records. `fd.read_try6` reads `try6.txt`, the record of the boot of the rerun: boot id, MemTotal, 12 memory modules, 7200 MT/s. It also reads `boots.txt` and `gaps.txt`. `fd.read_boot_table` reads the DIMM report: the module count of each earlier boot and the time until which the memory speed was 8000 MT/s. `state_of` (line 58) uses them for the earlier result folders only. `fd.read_log` reads the logs of go.sh and go2.sh.

Part A of the rerun: for each of the 3 sessions it finds the folder `R/k120-T72A1-<time>` (then T72A2, T72A3) and reads `probe.txt` and `threads120.csv`. The reader `fd.read_k120` keeps the rows whose column `rep` is a number. So it leaves out the `best` row and the column header row of each process [Ref1].

Parts L and C and control I: for each of the 9 folders `R/w120-<tag>-<time>` (tags T72L1 to T72L3, T72C1 to T72C4, T72I1, T72I2) it reads the one csv file, `env.txt` and `launches.txt`, and it takes the size of `stderr.txt`. `fd.read_bwx` stores the T rows by round, position and kernel. For each such group `fd.bwx_intervals` adds bytes / elapsed_s / 1e9 over the threads [Ref1].

It puts the 12 steps of the rerun (3 sessions of part A and 9 bwx12 processes) in time order. For each step it computes `gap_s`, the seconds from the end of the step before to the first launch of this step, and it builds a sentence that describes the start state.

It builds the records of the rerun. `add_k120` (line 119) appends one record per interval row of part A, with `GBps` = the csv column `aggregate_GBps`. `add_bwx` (line 142) appends one record per bwx12 interval, with `GBps` = the sum over the T rows. No interval of the rerun is left out: all kernels of every process become records.

It reads the 8000 MT/s baselines of part A and builds their records: A-1 (`threads120.csv` of 2026-11-13), A-2 (`A1.csv`) and A-3 (the 3 processes of `A3.csv` with the tags `onebuf-ms500-1` to `onebuf-ms500-3`). `open_probe13` reads the other records of the 2026-11-13 run.

It reads 17 csv files of 11 earlier data sets of bwx12 and bwx11 (L-1 to L-4, R0, R0b, X2d12, X1d10, X1d10b, BASEd10, F72d12) and builds their records. For 8 of these sets the filter `POS01` keeps only oldread at position 0 and asmread at position 1. For L-1, X2d12 and F72d12 every interval is kept.

It reads 8 data sets of the first runner bwx (files `B7.csv`, `C3.csv`, `B5.csv` in 6 folders). It keeps the sections whose tag starts with the prefix of the data set. In them it keeps only the kernels oldread, read and asmread (`READ3`).

It adds additional records that hold no rate of the rerun: the hardware error records of the 8000 MT/s boot (`hw_records`, `hw_compare`), the firmware settings (`open_fw`), the run before baseline A-2 (`open_a2pre`), and the proof of the module count (`open_mod`). Then `collect` returns `D`.

`main` calls `run_checks` (line 1036). It appends 27 checks to `D['checks']`. Each check has a key, a pass flag and one line of text. For the checks it also reads the three spec files, go.sh, go2.sh, ra.sh, rx.sh, run_kernels.sh, and the two checksum lists `local.sha` and `go2.sha`. The second readers read csv files again. stat_k120.py reads the part A files (for A-2 and A-3 the copies under `S/base8000`). stat_bwx.py reads the csv files of the 20 bwx12 and bwx11 folders. No second reader reads the csv files of the first runner bwx.

`main` calls `render` of `facts_text.py`. `render` computes the ranges, the medians and the percent values from the field `GBps` of the records. It returns the verdicts `V` and the text of FACTS.md [Ref2]. For the text, `render` and `section4` open two more input files: the rules file and `FINDINGS.md`. `render` ends the script here when a check failed, or when the data do not show the pattern of a sentence of the text [Ref11]. Then no output file is written.

`main` calls `write_json` (line 1038). It writes `S/facts.json` with three parts: `meta`, `verdicts`, and `intervals` (one line per record). Every float of the verdicts and of the records is rounded to 3 decimal places in this file.
`main` writes the text to `S/FACTS.md.tmp` and then renames that file to `S/FACTS.md`.

With `--print` it prints the text of FACTS.md. It prints the number of checks, the number of failed checks, one line per failed check, the number of records and the two verdicts. Line 1052 would end the script with the exit status 1 when a check failed. But `render` ends the script before these lines when a check failed. So in the present code they run only when every check passed. The script then prints `failed: 0` and ends with the exit status 0.

behavior_notes: **Rate of part A.** The script does not compute it. `add_k120` copies column 7 (`aggregate_GBps`) of each interval row of a part A csv into the field `GBps` (line 134). The csv is `threads120.csv`, or `A1.csv` and `A3.csv` for the baselines A-2 and A-3. The benchmark binary computed this value as the sum of the bytes of all threads divided by the longest per-thread elapsed time [Ref7]. The binary prints it with 2 decimal places (checked in the 216 interval rows of the 3 files of the rerun).

**Rate of the bwx runners (bwx12, bwx11, bwx).** `add_bwx` takes `GBps` from `fd.bwx_intervals` (lines 145 and 153). That function computes bytes / elapsed_s / 1e9 for each T row (one thread) and adds the values of all T rows with the same round, position and kernel [Ref1]. So the bytes of each thread are divided by the elapsed time of that thread. In a T row `bytes` is column 7, `elapsed_s` is column 8 and `cpu` is column 6 [Ref8]. `mesh0_GBps` is the same sum over the threads on CPUs 0-63. `mesh1_GBps` is the sum over the threads on CPUs 64 and above.

The two formulas differ. The field `rate_kind` of each record says which formula gave its `GBps`. The part A formula divides the bytes of all threads by one time, the longest per-thread time. The bwx formula divides the bytes of each thread by the time of that thread. So for the same threads the part A formula gives the lower value, or an equal one. Example from part A: the first interval row of `threads120.csv` of T72A1 (bw_old, kernel read) holds `aggregate_GBps` = 467.83 GB/s. Its column `per_thread_avg_GBps` holds 3.99 GB/s, the average of the 120 per-thread rates [Ref13]. The bwx formula would give the sum of these 120 rates: 120 x 3.99 GB/s = 478.8 GB/s (est., because the binary rounds the average to 0.01 GB/s) [Ref7]. Example from bwx12: the I row of an interval holds `aggregate_GBps`, which bwx12 computes with the part A formula [Ref8]. In the 9 files of the rerun the largest difference between this value and the sum over the T rows of the same interval is 0.018 GB/s (text of check `I-agg`, which prints 3 decimal places) [Ref9].

The column `aggregate_GBps` of the I row of a bwx csv is not used as the rate. Check `I-agg` (lines 736 to 740) compares it with the sum over the T rows of the same interval. The check passes when the largest difference in the 9 files of the rerun is below 0.05 GB/s. Example: in `a6456.csv` of T72L1 the I row of the first oldread interval holds 462.29 GB/s, and the 120 T rows of the same interval sum to 462.300 GB/s [Ref8].

**Rows that are left out.** Part A: the `best` row, the column header row and the per-thread rows (`thread,...`) of a process are not interval rows [Ref1]. A-3: only the processes of `A3.csv` with the tags `onebuf-ms500-1`, `-2`, `-3` are kept (line 189). Earlier folders of bwx12 and bwx11: only the csv files that the list `rx_sets` names give records (lines 207 to 221). These are 17 of the 52 csv files of the 11 folders. Data sets with the filter `POS01`: only oldread at position 0 and asmread at position 1 are kept (line 148). Data sets of the first runner bwx: only the sections whose tag starts with the prefix, and only the kernels of `READ3` (lines 276 and 280).
No row is left out because of its value. A T row with a flag other than `-` stays in the sum. The field `flagged` counts such rows.

**How the records name the two kernels.** Old read kernel: `binary` = `bw_old` with `kernel` = `read` in part A, and `kernel` = `oldread` in the bwx data sets. New read kernel: `binary` = `bw_new` with `kernel` = `read` in part A, and `kernel` = `read` in the bwx12 data sets. Among the bwx12 records only the data set `rerun-C` holds this kernel. The 8 data sets of the first runner bwx hold a kernel `read` too. The rules file counts it as the new read kernel, measured with another binary [Ref3]. Part L has no kernel `read`. The rules file uses asmread in its place there [Ref3].

**No statistics in this file.** This file computes no minimum, no median, no maximum and no percent drop of a kernel. `facts_text.py` and `facts_text4.py` compute them from the records [Ref2] [Ref11]. The only arithmetic on rates here is in the checks `I-agg` and `x-bwx` and in the hardware error view (`hw_compare`, `hw_compare_json`: rate of one round minus rate of the other round).

**Rounding.** The records in memory hold the values as parsed or summed. `facts_text.py` gets these unrounded values, and FACTS.md shows rates to 0.01 GB/s, rounded half up [Ref2]. In this file only `write_json` rounds, with the Python function `round`. Every float of the verdicts (through `r3all`) and of each record (line 1027) is rounded to 3 decimal places, which is 0.001 GB/s for a rate. In `meta` the rates and the interval times are rounded to 3 decimal places where they are built (lines 994 to 996 and `hw_compare_json`).

**How the rates are compared in the checks.** `x-k120` requires exact equality with the values that stat_k120.py reads: rate, per-thread minimum, per-thread maximum and pass count of every interval row (lines 799 to 815) [Ref5]. It also requires the same binary name and kernel name for every process. `x-k120` covers all 333 interval rows of part A that give a record: the 3 sessions of the rerun, A-1, A-2 and A-3. `x-bwx` requires that the total and the two sums per mesh differ from the values of stat_bwx.py by at most 1e-9 GB/s (lines 816 to 834) [Ref6]. It also requires the same result of the 64+56 test and the same number of flagged T rows for every interval. `x-bwx` covers the csv files that this script reads from the 9 folders of the rerun and from the 11 folders of the earlier bwx12 and bwx11 data sets: 26 files with 297 intervals. It covers every interval of these files, also the intervals that the filter `POS01` keeps out of the records. It does not cover the 8 data sets of the first runner bwx (312 records). Limit of both checks: they show that two readers take the same numbers from the same rows. They do not test the formula of the rate. stat_bwx.py uses the same formula as `fd.bwx_intervals`: the sum over the T rows of bytes / elapsed_s / 1e9 [Ref6]. `fd.read_k120` finds the `-- binary` header lines with the pattern `HDR`, which it takes from stat_k120.py [Ref1].

**The 27 checks, by key, in groups.** Logs and machine state: `log-go`, `log-go2`, `boot`, `memtotal`, `logins`, `uname`, `runnable`. Row counts and content of the files: `A-shape`, `A-order`, `I-rows`, `rc`, `stderr`, `6456`, `flags`, `P-rows`. Rates: `I-agg`, `x-k120`, `x-bwx`. Arguments: `args`, `args-R8`, `A-args`. Checksums: `sha-bw`, `sha-ra`, `sha-bwx12`, `sha-local`, `sha-rx`. Earlier data: `earlier`. All 27 passed in the build of 2026-11-17 [Ref9]. Since 2026-11-24 a new build fails `sha-local` (check 20 of the facts sheet). Line 20 of go.sh was edited on that day. So go.sh no longer has the sha256 that `local.sha` lists for it. The build then stops before it writes a file [Ref17].

**What the checksum checks of the binaries compare.** The binary files bw_old, bw_new and bwx12 are not in the local folders. So this file computes no sha256 of a binary. It compares values that the run scripts recorded on CRB. `sha-bw` (lines 753 to 760): the values of bw_old and bw_new in the 3 `probe.txt` files of part A must be equal to those in `probe.txt` of the first test of 2026-11-13 (folder `R/kernels-20261113T181222Z`). `env.txt` of the folder of A-2 must hold the same two values. `sha-bwx12` (lines 764 to 771): the 9 `env.txt` files of the rerun must hold one value, equal to the line `SHA=` of the local go.sh. `env.txt` of the 9 earlier bwx12 data sets must hold this value too. This file computes a sha256 itself only for local text files: go.sh, go2.sh, ra.sh, rx.sh, run_kernels.sh and the three spec files.

The order of the checks is the order of the `chk` calls in `run_checks`. FACTS.md numbers the checks in this order [Ref4]. The checks `sha-rx` and `A-args` were added last, at the end of the list. The comments at lines 844 and 867 give the reason: the numbers of the earlier checks stay as they were. The text of check `sha-rx` names check `sha-local` by its number. Line 866 computes this number from the position of `sha-local` in the list.

**A failed check stops the script before any file is written.** `run_checks` only records the result of each check. But `render` calls `section4` of `facts_text4.py`, and that function ends the script unless every check passed [Ref11]. This stop prints the message `facts_text.py: the data do not show the pattern of a sentence: all integrity checks pass`, and the exit status is 1. So the list `bad` of `main` (line 1044) is always empty in the present code. No `FAILED` line is printed (line 1047), and line 1052 (exit status 1) does not run. An `assert` that fails (29 `assert` statements in this file) also ends the script before any file is written. Every other stop inside `facts_data.py`, `facts_text.py` or `facts_text4.py` does the same. The reason: both files are written at the end of `main`.

**Records in the build of 2026-11-17: 793 records [Ref9].** rerun-A: 216 (3 sessions x 24 processes x 3 intervals). rerun-L: 30 (3 processes x 10 intervals). rerun-C: 24 (4 processes x 6 intervals). control-I: 20 (2 processes x 10 intervals). A-1: 72. A-2: 36. A-3: 9. The 11 earlier data sets of bwx12 and bwx11: 74. The 8 data sets of the first runner bwx: 312.

In part A the field `gap_s` is set on the records of the first process of a session only. ra.sh starts processes 2 to 24 directly after the process before (line 171). In session 1 the field is `None` for the first process too, because no step of the rerun ran before it.

The script reads its input files and changes none of them. It starts no benchmark and contacts no machine. It writes two files, `S/facts.json` and `S/FACTS.md`. Each is written under a temporary name and then renamed, so a reader never sees a part of a file. Line 23 tells Python to write no compiled copies of the imported modules (no `__pycache__` folder).

Every file opened through `fd._open` is added to the list `fd.OPENED`. `facts_text.py` stops when a file of this list is missing in the file list of FACTS.md section 7 [Ref2]. Lines 83, 234 and 805 add a file to the list with a direct `append` call, because the script takes only its size or another tool opens it. The list does not hold every file that is read. stat_bwx.py opens every csv file of a folder with its own `open` call. So for check `x-bwx` it also reads 35 csv files of the earlier folders that this script does not read, for example `a0001.csv` in the folder of L-1. Their rows are not compared, and they give no record. `section4` opens `FINDINGS.md` with its own `open` call too. `facts_text.py` adds that file to the file list directly [Ref2].

words.def: the Arm reference server under test. It has 128 CPUs.
the two halves of the chip. CPUs 0-63 sit on mesh 0. CPUs 64-127 sit on mesh 1.
our runs use CPUs 0-119 only: 64 threads on mesh 0 plus 56 threads on mesh 1. Each thread reads its own buffer of 256 MiB from memory.
million transfers per second, the unit of memory speed.
the whole-chip read test of 2026-11-17 on CRB, run after the memory speed was lowered from 8000 MT/s to 7200 MT/s. go.sh ran parts A, L and C. go2.sh ran control I afterwards.
one memory module (DIMM = dual in-line memory module). CRB has 12 slots.
the inner loop of the benchmark that reads memory. On this page "kernel" means this loop. The operating system kernel is always written "Linux kernel".
portable C code with 16 running sums. Each load is followed by an add. Its name is `read` in the binary bw_old and `oldread` in the runner bwx12.
NEON intrinsics (C functions that map to Arm vector instructions), loads only. Its name is `read` in the binary bw_new and `read` in bwx12.
a hand-written load-only loop. It has the same 8 "ldp q" loads per 256 B as the new read kernel. "ldp q" is the Arm instruction that loads two 16-byte vector registers.
the new read kernel or asmread.
test loops of bwx12: the asmread loop with 96 or 256 no-operation instructions per 256 B, and a loop with one load per 64 B line.
the benchmark and its two binaries of 2026-11-13. bw_old was built from the old source, bw_new from the new source.
later runner programs for the same loops. They print one row per thread. bwx12 is the runner of the 2026-11-15 investigation. bwx11 and bwx are older versions.

a process is one start of a benchmark binary. An interval is one timed measurement inside a process. bwx12 times a sequence of kernels and repeats the sequence: each repeat is a round (counted from 0), and the position is the place of a kernel in the sequence (counted from 0). In part A the round (1 or 2) is the round of the script: round 2 runs the processes in the reverse order.
one pass of go.sh through part A, part L and part C.
the 120-thread part of the test of 2026-11-13, repeated with the same two binaries.
one bwx12 process with the kernel sequence oldread, asmread, read_nop96, read_nop256, read_1pl.
one bwx12 process with the sequence oldread, read, asmread (cfwd) or asmread, read, oldread (crev).
the part L line, started from an idle machine, twice. It was added after the first numbers were seen. It is not part of the plan fixed before the run.
the arguments of one bwx12 process, as a spec file holds them. "The same line" means a process with the same arguments.
a launch at a 1-minute load average below 1.0.
a line that go.sh or go2.sh prints with the time, the boot id, MemTotal, the load, the logins and the processes per user.

the row kinds of a bwx csv file: one I row per interval, one T row per thread and interval, one P row per thread before the first interval and after each interval (it holds the page state of the buffer), and one C row per thread and interval with counter values. The C rows exist only for a process that ran with the counter option `--count`.
the stop rule of bandwidth.c: after the minimum time (0.5 s here) each thread finishes the pass over its buffer that it is in. The threads stop at different times.
the stop rule used with bwx12 here: all threads stop at the same time (after 6 s).
a random identifier that Linux creates at each start. Equal boot ids mean the same boot.
the usable memory that Linux reports, in kB.
GB = 1e9 bytes. Every rate is in GB/s.
estimated, not measured directly.

`R` = `/home/jhan/workspace/titan/cache-perf/crb/results`, the result folders copied back from CRB. `S` = `/home/jhan/workspace/titan/cache-perf/crb/tmp/agent-scratch/w120-7200-2026-11-17`, the folder of this script. Both names come from `facts_data.py`.
two folders next to `S`. `w120-2026-11-15` holds rx.sh and r0.sh. `kernels-2026-11-13` holds run_kernels.sh.
the module `facts_data.py`, imported under this short name. It holds the parsers of the raw files and small helpers (`rel`, `sel`, `find`, `sha256`, `clock`). It writes nothing.
the list in `facts_data.py` of the input files that were opened through `fd._open`. Lines 83, 234 and 805 of this script add more files to it. The file list of FACTS.md is checked against it.

the dictionary that `collect` builds and that every later step reads. Main keys: `recs` (all interval records), `checks`, `A` (the 3 part A folders of the rerun), `X` (the 9 bwx12 folders of the rerun), `events` (the 12 steps in time order), `base`, `rx`, `step` (earlier data sets), `logs`, `try6`.
one Python dictionary per timed interval, made by `fd.base_record`. Every record has the same 40 keys. The list `D['recs']` holds all records. facts.json stores them under `intervals`.
the field of a record that holds the rate of the interval in GB/s. Part A: the csv column `aggregate_GBps`. bwx runners: the sum over the T rows of bytes / elapsed_s / 1e9.
a column that the benchmark binary prints per interval: the sum of the bytes of all threads, divided by the longest per-thread elapsed time, in GB/s.

part A only: total_bytes / bytes_per_thread of an interval row, as a whole number. For copy and asmcopy the value is 2 x the number of buffer passes, because the binary counts read plus written bytes for these two kernels.

the field that says which group of runs a record belongs to. The rerun has `rerun-A`, `rerun-L`, `rerun-C` and `control-I`. Every earlier group has a short label. The entries below list these labels. The field `part` (A, L, C or I) says to which part of the test a record belongs: the earlier bwx12 and bwx11 data sets carry L, and the data sets of the first runner bwx carry C.

the field that says how a data set is used: rerun, control, baseline, supporting, other binary, not a baseline, or 10 modules. F72d12 has its own value: a 7200 MT/s sample of the same boot that is not part of the rerun.
an 8000 MT/s run with 12 memory modules that the rules file names as the comparison for a part of the rerun.

the 8000 MT/s baselines of part A, all of 2026-11-13. A-1 = `threads120.csv` of `R/kernels-20261113T181222Z` (the first test). A-2 = `A1.csv` of `R/partA-20261113T205055Z`. A-3 = 3 processes of `A3.csv` of the same folder (old read kernel only).

the 8000 MT/s rows of bwx12. L-1 (folder `w120-R8-...`) has the same argument line as part L. L-2, L-3 and L-4 are supporting runs of 4 s with other counter events. Of them only oldread at position 0 and asmread at position 1 are used.
rows of the other binary bwx11 at 8000 MT/s.
bwx12 runs that are not baselines. X2d12 ran with a firmware test setting. The other three ran in boots with 10 memory modules.
an earlier run of the like.spec line in the same 7200 MT/s boot, about 2 h 10 min before the rerun. It is not part of the rerun.

words.term: B7a, B7b, C3a, C3b, B5a, B5b, B5a-rev, B5b-rev
words.def: runs of the first runner bwx at 8000 MT/s (2026-11-13 and 2026-11-14). One csv file holds several processes. The two `-rev` sets hold the kernels in reverse order.

words.term: Rules file, rules V1 and V4
words.def: the file `S/baselines-and-rules.txt`, written before the rerun started. V4 fixes the list of the 8000 MT/s baselines. V1 point 2 fixes the comparison: the range from minimum to maximum at 7200 MT/s against the same range at 8000 MT/s. The script does not read the list of the baselines from this file. The folders and files of the earlier data sets are written in the code of `collect` (lines 184 to 189, 207 to 221 and 258 to 267). `render` opens the file and uses its line 2, which holds the writing time [Ref2].

the facts sheet of the investigation of 2026-11-15 into the drop of the read rate. It lies in the folder `w120-2026-11-15` next to `S`. `section4` reads its section F2 and searches it for names of test loops. No number is taken from it.
the set of the two pairs (oldread, position 0) and (asmread, position 1). As a filter it keeps only these two intervals of each round.
the three kernel names oldread, read and asmread.

the Markdown text that this script writes. Its section 3 answers Q1 and its section 4 answers Q2. The report script make_report.py does not take its numbers from this text. It computes them from the records of facts.json and from the raw csv files. Then it compares them with this text [Ref16].

the JSON output file of this script. `meta` describes the run and holds the checks. `verdicts` holds the answers. `intervals` holds one record per timed interval. The report script make_report.py reads this file.

the two questions of the rerun. Q1: at 7200 MT/s with 12 memory modules, is the whole-chip read rate of the new read kernel still below that of the old read kernel, and by how much. Q2: did either kernel's rate differ from the earlier runs with 12 modules at 8000 MT/s [Ref4].
the dictionary that `render` of `facts_text.py` returns. `V['q1']` and `V['q2']` are the answer sentences to Q1 and Q2. `write_json` stores `V` under `verdicts`.

the second file of the text code. `render` of `facts_text.py` calls its function `section4` for sections 4 to 6 of FACTS.md. `section4` ends the script with an error message unless every check passed [Ref11].
one entry of `D['checks']`: a key such as `I-agg`, a pass flag `ok`, and one line of text with the counted values. FACTS.md prints the checks in its section 1.4.

the two driver scripts of the rerun. go.sh ran 3 sessions and then one more part C process. go2.sh ran control I. Each printed state lines. The scripts name no log file. The command that started each script on CRB sent its standard output and its error output into the log [Ref14]. The last line of a complete log is `ALLDONE`.
the function of go.sh and go2.sh that prints a line `FAILED: <reason>`, prints a state line and ends the script with the exit status 1.

two lists of sha256 values in `S`. `local.sha` lists go.sh, ra.sh and the three spec files. `go2.sha` lists go2.sh. The AI agent (Claude Code) that ran the rerun wrote each list on its own server from the local files. The same command line then copied the files and the list to CRB and tested the copies there with `sha256sum -c` [Ref14]. Check `sha-local` tests the present local files against the two lists. Since 2026-11-24 it fails for go.sh.
the script of part A. It starts 24 processes one after the other: 2 rounds x 6 kernels x 2 binaries (bw_old, bw_new), each with 3 intervals of at least 0.5 s.

rx.sh starts one process of the binary that it is given (bwx12 in the rerun) for each line of a spec file. It writes the result folder `w120-<name>-<time>`. r0.sh is the earlier runner script of the data set R0 (binary bwx11). It wrote no `binary` line into env.txt, so this script takes the checksum from the text of r0.sh.
the script of the first test of 2026-11-13. Its 120-thread part is what part A repeats.
the function of ra.sh and of run_kernels.sh that writes the `-- binary` header line and then starts one benchmark process with `--reps 3 --min-ms 500` (3 intervals of at least 500 ms each).
the scripts that wrote the result folders `partA-...`, `B7-...`, `C3-...` and `B5-...` of 2026-11-13 and 2026-11-14. Their csv files hold one header line `-- step ...` per process.
the lines of one process inside a csv file of the first runner bwx. Each section starts with a `-- step ...` header line. A csv file of rx.sh has one section.

the result file of part A. Per process it holds one header line `-- binary ...` that ra.sh writes, one `# bandwidth:` line and one column header row that the binary prints, one row per interval (3 here), and one `best` row.
a row of a part A csv whose column 4 (`rep`) is a number: one row per timed interval. The `best` row, the column header row and the per-thread rows (`thread,...`) are not interval rows.

the state file that ra.sh writes into a part A folder: time, load, logins, boot id, MemTotal, runnable tasks, Linux kernel release, a process list, the sha256 values of bw_old, bw_new and ra.sh, and one `load_after` line at the end of the session [Ref10].

files that rx.sh writes into a bwx folder. env.txt: date, Linux kernel release, load, the logged-in users, a process list, and the line `binary <path> <sha256>`. launches.txt: one `launch` line directly before each process (tag, time, load, logins, arguments) and one `rc` line after it. stderr.txt: the error output of the processes. The script reads only its size [Ref10].
the exit status of a benchmark process, as rx.sh writes it into launches.txt with the end time. `rc 0` means that the process ended without an error.
a file with one line `tag|arguments`. rx.sh starts one bwx12 process with these arguments. like.spec is the line of part L and of control I. cfwd.spec and crev.spec are the two lines of part C.

a short name. A folder tag such as T72A1, T72L2, T72C4 or T72I1 names one step of the rerun: the part and the session or process number. A process tag such as `a6456` is the first field of a spec line and the name of the csv file.
one entry of `D['events']`: one session of part A (24 processes) or one bwx12 process. The rerun has 12 steps.

`gap_s` is the time in seconds from the end of the previous step of the rerun to the first launch of this step, at 1 s resolution. The start state is a sentence built from it, for example "started 5 s after the 120-thread bwx12 process T72L1". The first step (T72A1) has no `gap_s`. Its sentence is built from the seconds since the first state line of the go.sh log.

the kernel that was timed directly before an interval. bwx runners: the previous kernel of the sequence in the same process (for position 0 of round 1 it is the last kernel of the sequence). Part A: binary and kernel of the previous process in the same csv file. The first interval of a bwx process and the first process of a part A file get a text that starts with `none`. In A-3 the second and the third process get the text `not listed (other processes of the file ran in between)`, because the list holds 3 of the 12 processes of `A3.csv` (lines 124 to 129).
a text that is equal for all records of one process: folder, file, and the process number or the tag.
true when an interval has 64 T rows on CPUs 0-63 and 56 T rows on CPUs 64-119, on 120 different CPUs.

the last column of a T row. `-` means no flag. `flagged` is the number of T rows of an interval with another value. stat_bwx.py says that the runner writes `late` for a thread that started more than 100 us (microseconds) after the common start.
transparent huge pages, the Linux feature that puts a buffer on 2 MiB pages. In a P row `kB_total` is the size of the buffer and `kB_huge` is the part of it on huge pages [Ref12].

a column of a P row. bwx12 copies it from the Linux file `/proc/vmstat`, where it counts for the whole system [Ref12]. Linux adds 1 to it when a page fault cannot get a huge page and uses small pages in its place [Ref15]. Check `P-rows` prints its values and does not test them.
the number of tasks that are runnable or wait for disk input and output, averaged by Linux over the last 1, 5 and 15 minutes. `load1` is the 1-minute value.
the first number of the fourth field of `/proc/loadavg`: the tasks that are runnable at that moment.
the number of logged-in users. The run scripts count them with `who | wc -l`.
the file `/tmp/positron-perf.RUNNING` on CRB. The run scripts stop when it exists. A state line says `marker absent` or `marker present`.
the time from the `launch` line to the `rc` line of a process in launches.txt. Both lines give whole seconds.
the version text of the operating system kernel, as the command `uname -r` prints it.
a checksum of a file, written as 64 hexadecimal digits. Equal values mean equal file content.

the file `R/dimm7200-20261117/try6.txt`, written about 2 h 10 min before the rerun in the same boot. It holds the time, the boot id, MemTotal, the Linux message "This system has 12 DIMM sockets", and a count line: 12 entries with "Configured Memory Speed: 7200 MT/s". The module count of the records comes from the DIMM sockets line.

the three fields that every record of the rerun gets: `speed_MTps` = 7200, `modules` = 12 and `boot` = the boot id of the rerun. The values are read from `try6.txt`. The records of F72d12 get the same three fields. The folder of F72d12 holds no boot id. Line 242 requires that its process ran between two readings of this boot id: `try6.txt` before it, and the first state line of the go.sh log after it.

two files in `R/dimm7200-20261117`. boots.txt lists the boots of the journal, one per row, with a boot number, the boot id, a first time and a last time. gaps.txt gives per boot the first and the last time of the Linux kernel log, a DIMM count and the number after `hwerr=`. Row 0 of boots.txt holds the boot id of the rerun, and the script takes row 0 of gaps.txt as the same boot. The last time of each row 0 is the time at which the file was written (20:06:19 and 20:06:34 UTC), about 2 h before the rerun.

the file `/home/jhan/workspace/machines/arm-crb/DIMM-flaky-report.md`, outside `R`. Its boot table lists each boot with a number, the Linux start time and the module count. It also gives the time until which the memory speed was 8000 MT/s.

saved system logs of one boot in `R/dimm-check-20261117`. `h-5.txt` (journal) and `k-5.txt` (Linux kernel log) belong to the boot that started on 2026-11-09. Every baseline ran in that boot [Ref3]. `h-1.txt` and `k-1.txt` belong to a boot of 2026-11-17 with 10 modules.

the file `R/dimm7200-20261117/dmi17-7200.txt`, saved in the boot of the rerun. It is output of the tool `dmidecode`, which prints the hardware table of the firmware. It holds 12 entries `Memory Device`, each with lines such as `Size: 32 GB` and `Configured Memory Speed: 7200 MT/s`.

the dictionary that `open_mod` returns: the DIMM sockets message of a boot with 10 modules, the line `Memory: ...K/...K available` of two Linux kernel logs, line counts of the module list, and the value and the line number of the line `modules=` of `try6.txt`.
one journal line "Hardware error from APEI Generic Hardware Error Source" (APEI = ACPI Platform Error Interface). A later line with the same record number gives the severity, for example "corrected".

words.term: Span of a hardware error record
words.def: the range from `off` - 1 to `off` + 1 seconds after the process start, where `off` is the journal time of the record minus the launch time. The record lies somewhere in this range, because both times are whole seconds.
the interval with the same kernel and the same position in the other round of the same process.

a tool that reads and sets firmware settings. `questions.json` is a saved list of all settings (name, answer, options, help). `set.txt` holds the replies of the `set` calls. "DIMM Frequency" is the setting of the memory speed.

two firmware settings. The `set` calls saved in the folder `R/fwtest-20261117` changed them and then set them back. Their help texts say: maximum and minimum outstanding TXREQ transactions from the L2 transaction queue. FACTS.md describes the TXREQ settings as firmware settings that limit the read requests of the cores [Ref4].

a file of the folder `R/dimm7200-20261117` with one line: `answer: "7200 MT/s",`. The comment of `open_fw` calls it the last reading of the memory speed setting. The line itself does not name the setting.
the first part of the test of 2026-11-13: processes with one thread, run before the 120-thread part. Its result file is `one-thread.csv`. The rerun did not repeat it.

the dictionary that `open_probe13` returns: the sha256 values and the times of `probe.txt` of 2026-11-13, the number and the times of the header lines of the one-thread phase, facts of the journal of that boot (start, module count, hardware error records in the time spans of the baselines), and saved machine settings.
two smaller statistics tools in `S`. stat_k120.py reads `threads120.csv`. stat_bwx.py reads bwx csv files. This script uses them as a second reader (checks `x-k120` and `x-bwx`).

another script that reads the same data with its own code (stat_k120.py or stat_bwx.py). A check compares its values with the values of this script. For A-2 and A-3 stat_k120.py reads the copies under `S/base8000`, and this script reads the raw files.

a folder with two copies in the form of `threads120.csv`, read by stat_k120.py. `partA-A1` is `A1.csv` (baseline A-2) with the header line of each process rewritten into the `-- binary` form. `partA-A3-onebuf500` holds the three processes of baseline A-3 in the same form. Inside these processes only the header lines differ from the raw files.

functions.name: iso
functions.what: Formats a date and time as text such as `2026-11-17T22:12:14Z`.

functions.name: r3
functions.what: Rounds a number to 3 decimal places. Returns `None` for `None`.

functions.name: boot_of
functions.what: Returns the last boot of the DIMM report table whose Linux start time is not after the time `t`.

functions.name: collect
functions.what: Reads the raw result files and the saved machine records. Returns `D`: interval records, rerun folders, baselines, steps in time order, additional records.

functions.name: state_of
functions.what: Nested in `collect`. Returns memory speed, module count and boot label of an earlier result folder, from the boot table of the DIMM report.

functions.name: add_k120
functions.what: Nested in `collect`. Appends one record per interval row of bandwidth.c processes. `GBps` is the csv column `aggregate_GBps`, copied unchanged.

functions.name: add_bwx
functions.what: Nested in `collect`. Appends one record per interval of a bwx section. `GBps` is the sum over its T rows. Optional kernel and position filters.

functions.name: hw_records
functions.what: Finds the hardware error records of the saved journal inside the process windows of L-1 to L-4, R0, R0b. Tests each record against each interval.

functions.name: hw_compare
functions.what: For each interval with an error record: the rate minus the rate of the same kernel and position in the other round of the process.

functions.name: other
functions.what: Nested in `hw_compare`. Returns the interval with the same position and kernel in the other round.

functions.name: cmp_
functions.what: Nested in `hw_compare`. Returns an interval, its partner of the other round, and the difference of the two rates in GB/s.

functions.name: hw_compare_json
functions.what: Turns the result of `hw_compare` into the form that facts.json stores. Rates are rounded to 0.001 GB/s.

functions.name: open_fw
functions.what: Reads the saved firmware setting lists and the replies of the settings tool under `R`. Checks that no other such file exists.

functions.name: open_a2pre
functions.what: Reads the times and the process header lines of the run folder that ended shortly before the first process of baseline A-2.

functions.name: open_mod
functions.what: Reads what a boot with 10 modules shows in journal and Linux kernel log, and the module list saved in the boot of the rerun.

functions.name: open_probe13
functions.what: Reads the records of the 2026-11-13 run: checksums and times of probe.txt, the one-thread phase, error records of the journal, saved machine settings.

functions.name: run_checks
functions.what: Appends 27 integrity checks to `D['checks']`: logs, boot id, row counts, thread placement, checksums, arguments, and two cross-checks of the rates.

functions.name: chk
functions.what: Nested in `run_checks`. Appends one check: key, pass flag, text.

functions.name: per
functions.what: Nested in `run_checks`. Builds a text such as `T72L1 10, T72L2 10` from a list of rerun folders and a function.

functions.name: write_json
functions.what: Writes facts.json: `meta`, `verdicts`, and one line per interval record. Floats of verdicts and records are rounded to 3 decimal places.

functions.name: r3all
functions.what: Nested in `write_json`. Rounds every float inside nested dictionaries and lists to 3 decimal places.

functions.name: main
functions.what: Entry point. Collects, checks, renders, writes facts.json and FACTS.md, prints check counts and verdicts. A failed check stops the script in `render`, before the writes.

refs.what: `read_k120` (lines 264 to 304) reads the interval rows of part A. `read_bwx` (lines 313 to 353) stores the T rows by round, position and kernel. `bwx_intervals` (lines 356 to 383) adds the T rows of each interval. `base_record` (lines 421 to 433) lists the keys of a record. Line 271 of `read_k120` matches the `-- binary` header line with the pattern `HDR` of stat_k120.py.

`analyse` (line 283), `compare` (line 333) and `render` (line 341) compute the pairs, ranges, medians and percent values from the records. `g` (line 46) formats a rate to 0.01 GB/s, rounded half up. Lines 1474 and 1475 compare `fd.OPENED` with the file list of FACTS.md. Line 186 of `register` adds `FINDINGS.md` to that file list. Lines 380 to 388 read line 2 of the rules file: `render` stops when the writing time in that line is not before the first state line of the go.sh log.

Line 18 says that every baseline ran in the boot of 2026-11-09 with 12 memory modules at 8000 MT/s. The fixed list of the 8000 MT/s baselines (lines 21 to 43, asmread in place of the new read kernel in line 36) and rule V1 (lines 70 to 82). Lines 40 and 78 name the kernel `read` of the runner bwx as the nearest data for the new read kernel of part C.
The word list (lines 38 to 89), the questions Q1 and Q2 (lines 95 and 96), and the 27 check lines of section 1.4 (lines 213 to 239).
`load` (lines 24 to 44) reads the interval rows of a `threads120.csv` a second time.

`read_csv` (lines 38 to 58) computes bytes / elapsed_s / 1e9 for each T row (line 54). `interval_rows` (lines 61 to 81) computes total, sums per mesh, the 64+56 test and the flagged count a second time.
Lines 1 to 7: the header line of ra.sh, the `# bandwidth:` line with the formula of `aggregate_GBps`, the column names, 3 interval rows and the `best` row.

Lines 1 to 6: the header lines with the column names of the I, T, P and C rows. Line 1 gives the formula of `aggregate_GBps`: sum(bytes) / max(per-thread elapsed_s). Line 128: the I row of round 0, position 0 (oldread). Lines 129 to 248: its 120 T rows.
`meta.counts`: 793 records and the count per data set. `meta.checks`: 27 checks, all with `ok` true (file written 2026-11-17 at 20:55 local time, which is 2026-11-18 04:55 UTC).

Line 17 writes a state line. Lines 40 to 46 give the order of the steps. `ra.sh` (same folder, lines 30 to 36 and 49) writes probe.txt. `rx.sh` (folder `w120-2026-11-15`, lines 10, 16 and 20) writes env.txt and launches.txt.

`section4` (from line 24) writes sections 4 to 6 of FACTS.md. Line 1461 ends the script unless every check passed. It uses `need` of `facts_text.py` (line 36), which raises `SystemExit` with a message. `render` calls `section4` at line 1464 of `facts_text.py`. `section4` also computes ranges from the records. For this it calls `rng` of `facts_data.py` (lowest value, highest value and median of a list of records) and `compare` of `facts_text.py`, for example at lines 51 and 81.

`read_smaps` (lines 1515 to 1542) takes `kB_total` from the line `Size:` and `kB_huge` from the line `AnonHugePages:` of the entry of the buffer in `/proc/self/smaps`. `read_vmstat` (lines 1545 to 1560) reads four counters of `/proc/vmstat`, among them `thp_fault_fallback`. The comment at line 1544 says that they count for the whole system.

Lines 427 to 446 (source of bw_old) print an interval row. `aggregate_GBps` = total bytes / longest per-thread time / 1e9, printed with 2 decimal places. `per_thread_avg_GBps` = the sum of the per-thread rates bytes / elapsed_s / 1e9, divided by the thread count. `bandwidth.c` of the same folder (source of bw_new) holds the same code in lines 584 to 603. This local text of `bandwidth.c` has the sha256 `f1985072...`. `probe.txt` of the build-only run of 18:32:18 UTC on 2026-11-13 (`R/kernels-20261113T183218Z`, line 15) holds this value. `probe.txt` of the timed run of 18:12:22 UTC (`R/kernels-20261113T181222Z`, line 15) holds another sha256 for `bandwidth.c` (`c1406e02...`). All three `probe.txt` records of that day hold the same sha256 for the binary bw_new (`fd7c14df...`). ra.sh checks this value. So the machine code is not in doubt. The two texts differ in comment lines only. An edit of 2026-11-13 18:32:07 UTC replaced 2 comment lines above `k_read` with the 5 comment lines 178 to 182 of the local text. The record of the Claude Code session of that day holds the edit (`/home/jhan/.claude/projects/-home-jhan-workspace-titan-cache-perf-crb/7663f0d2-7d09-4571-b80c-92526358fa86.jsonl`, line 1000). With this edit reversed, the local text has the sha256 value of the earlier text (c1406e02...). No code line differs.

The record of the Claude Code session of 2026-11-17, one JSON record per line. It lies outside the project folder. Line 313 holds the command that started go.sh on CRB, and line 365 the command that started go2.sh. Both have the form `nohup setsid SCRIPT > $L 2>&1 < /dev/null &`, where `L` is the path of the log. The part `> $L 2>&1` sends the standard output and the error output of the script into the log. Line 309 holds the command line that wrote `local.sha`, copied go.sh, ra.sh, the three spec files and the list to CRB, and ran `sha256sum -c local.sha` there. Line 353 holds the same steps for go2.sh and `go2.sha`.

External source: Linux kernel documentation, page "Transparent Hugepage Support" (docs.kernel.org/admin-guide/mm/transhuge.html), section "Monitoring usage". It lists `thp_fault_fallback` among the counters of `/proc/vmstat`. It says that the counter is incremented if a page fault fails to allocate or charge a huge page and instead falls back to using small pages.

The header text (lines 5 to 12) names facts.json as the input. It says that the function `val` sums the thread rows of the raw csv for the last digit of a bwx rate, and that the computed values are compared with FACTS.md.

tests of 2026-11-24 for the edit of line 20 of go.sh. The files that end with `.out` hold their output. `go.sh.as-run-2026-11-17` is a copy of go.sh from before the edit. `check_line20.py` reads the local go.sh and puts the old line back in a copy of the text in memory. It does not change the file. That text has the sha256 that `local.sha` lists for go.sh. `check_facts_build.py` runs this script in a copy of `S`. With the edited go.sh the build ends with status 1 and writes no file. With the old line 20 it passes.
